subject: The Intelligent Investor: Leverage or Luck?

96 If you buy and hold a leveraged ETF, anything can happen.   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Jason Zweig   Leverage or Luck?   If you buy and hold a leveraged ETF, anything can happen.     Jean-François Millet, "The Quarriers" (1846-1847) TOLEDO MUSEUM OF ART, GIFT OF ARTHUR J. SECOR   Fellow investors,

   In my Sept. 4 column, “You’re Not Tough Enough to Earn These Huge Returns,” I explored whether holding leveraged ETFs for the long run is a good idea.

   These funds typically seek to double or even triple the daily returns of underlying assets such as broad market indexes, commodities, cryptocurrencies and single stocks. Over longer horizons, though, leveraged ETFs can deviate sharply from the assets they track—often resulting in titanic gains or devastating losses.

   As I wrote in the column :

   Advocates of leveraged ETFs for the long run are fond of pointing to ProShares UltraPro QQQ, a leveraged ETF known as TQQQ that seeks to triple the daily return of the technology-dominated Nasdaq-100 index. Since TQQQ launched in 2010, it has returned nearly 35,000%. That otherworldly gain is light-years ahead of the Nasdaq-100’s more than 1,800% return.

   Then I added:

   Who earned that gigantic cumulative return? My best guess is: absolutely nobody.
In the worst five weeks of the market’s response to Covid-19 in 2020, the Nasdaq-100 index fell 27.8%.
TQQQ lost 69.8%.
In 2022, the index dropped 32.4%.
TQQQ lost 79%.
Between mid-February and early April 2025, the Nasdaq-100 was down 22.8%.
TQQQ lost 56.9%.
The human mind isn’t made to withstand that much short-term pain, no matter how much greater the potential long-term gain might be.

   To which a couple of readers responded: Oh yeah? My mind is made to withstand it! They sent along screenshots of their brokerage accounts to prove it.

   Christopher Bray emailed:

   My wife would be happy to report to you that in 2010, I invested a fair portion of her very tiny Roth IRA in TQQQ. Over the years I’ve consistently sold large portions of it to diversify, but her Roth IRA still holds 1,920 shares with a cost basis of $0.23 per share for a total return of almost 32,000%.
In hindsight, I kick myself for selling any of it over the years.

   Ellen Ching emailed that she had invested ”a little over $3,000” in TQQQ in 2014 and that it’s now worth more than $150,000. She added:

   As my numbers demonstrate, TQQQ is one of the best wealth-building vehicles, especially for younger investors who can put aside their investments for long periods of time, and if this investment is no more than a small percentage of their total portfolio….As long as investors can stomach some volatility, it really is a good investment.

   My response is simple. Returns are period-dependent. How well you do always depends largely on when you start counting and when you stop. Because leverage multiplies your returns both on the way up and the way down, it turbocharges that basic fact.

   Every once in a while, a leveraged fund gets completely wiped out . Although such total goose eggs are rare, an inverse 3X fund that sought to triple the opposite of the daily return of Moderna stock went to zero last month on the London Stock Exchange. Total loss is less likely with lower leverage and broader underlying assets.

   TQQQ launched Feb. 9, 2010, less than a year after stocks bottomed in the global financial crisis and a decade after the bubble in internet stocks burst.

   That was a pretty good time to start counting! So was 2014, when my second reader bought in.

   TQQQ isn’t old enough to have gone through two of the worst market bloodbaths in history. From the end of October 2007 to early March 2009, the Nasdaq-100 index lost 51.6%. From March 2000 to early October 2002, it sank a terrifying 82.4%.

   How would a leveraged fund have performed if it had existed long enough to suffer multiples of those losses?

   Many investors might not know that TQQQ has an older, slightly more conservative sibling: UltraNasdaq-100 ProFund. It’s a mutual fund, not an ETF, and it seeks to double rather than triple the Nasdaq-100 index’s daily returns.

   Its track record just so happens to include both the global financial crisis and the bursting of the internet bubble.

   The results (the fund is in blue, the index in green) are not pretty:

     Performance of the UltraNasdaq-100 ProFund and the Nasdaq-100 index FACTSET   The leveraged fund earned an annualized average of 1.6 percentage points less than the underlying index over the long run—a cumulative gulf of more than 590 percentage points.

   This period includes the full year of 1999, when the Nasdaq-100 doubled and the fund more than tripled.

   To be fair, the mutual fund has much higher expenses than the TQQQ ETF, accounting for part of its underperformance—but not all.

   So, if you bought TQQQ in 2010 or 2014 and have held it ever since, you are tough, and you’ve earned the right to crow about it. But you’re also lucky.

   The past decade-and-a-half have been a Golden Age for leveraged funds: Interest rates were at rock-bottom until recently, and stocks boomed. But no Golden Age lasts forever, especially in markets. If rates keep going up and markets go down, the same leverage that magnified wealth on the way up will destroy it on the way down.

     Archimedes lifting the world with a lever, detail from the cover of Mechanic's Magazine, vol. 2 (London, 1824) UNIVERSITY OF PENNSYLVANIA LIBRARIES   This is an edition of the Intelligent Investor newsletter, where Jason Zweig writes twice monthly about investment strategy and how to think about money. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here .

   Is this market like 1999 all over again? More like 1901, I argued in “ What a 125-Year-Old Bull Market Says About Today’s Trading Craze .”

Leverage or Luck?
 
If you buy and hold a leveraged ETF, anything can happen.
 
 
Jean-François Millet, "The Quarriers" (1846-1847) TOLEDO MUSEUM OF ART, GIFT OF ARTHUR J. SECOR
 

Fellow investors,

 

In my Sept. 4 column, “You’re Not Tough Enough to Earn These Huge Returns,” I explored whether holding leveraged ETFs for the long run is a good idea.

 

These funds typically seek to double or even triple the daily returns of underlying assets such as broad market indexes, commodities, cryptocurrencies and single stocks. Over longer horizons, though, leveraged ETFs can deviate sharply from the assets they track—often resulting in titanic gains or devastating losses.

 

As I wrote in the column:

 

Advocates of leveraged ETFs for the long run are fond of pointing to ProShares UltraPro QQQ, a leveraged ETF known as TQQQ that seeks to triple the daily return of the technology-dominated Nasdaq-100 index. Since TQQQ launched in 2010, it has returned nearly 35,000%. That otherworldly gain is light-years ahead of the Nasdaq-100’s more than 1,800% return.

 

Then I added:

 

Who earned that gigantic cumulative return? My best guess is: absolutely nobody.
In the worst five weeks of the market’s response to Covid-19 in 2020, the Nasdaq-100 index fell 27.8%.
TQQQ lost 69.8%.
In 2022, the index dropped 32.4%.
TQQQ lost 79%.
Between mid-February and early April 2025, the Nasdaq-100 was down 22.8%.
TQQQ lost 56.9%.
The human mind isn’t made to withstand that much short-term pain, no matter how much greater the potential long-term gain might be.

 

To which a couple of readers responded: Oh yeah? My mind is made to withstand it! They sent along screenshots of their brokerage accounts to prove it.

 

Christopher Bray emailed:

 

My wife would be happy to report to you that in 2010, I invested a fair portion of her very tiny Roth IRA in TQQQ. Over the years I’ve consistently sold large portions of it to diversify, but her Roth IRA still holds 1,920 shares with a cost basis of $0.23 per share for a total return of almost 32,000%.
In hindsight, I kick myself for selling any of it over the years.

 

Ellen Ching emailed that she had invested ”a little over $3,000” in TQQQ in 2014 and that it’s now worth more than $150,000. She added:

 

As my numbers demonstrate, TQQQ is one of the best wealth-building vehicles, especially for younger investors who can put aside their investments for long periods of time, and if this investment is no more than a small percentage of their total portfolio….As long as investors can stomach some volatility, it really is a good investment.

 

My response is simple. Returns are period-dependent. How well you do always depends largely on when you start counting and when you stop. Because leverage multiplies your returns both on the way up and the way down, it turbocharges that basic fact.

 

Every once in a while, a leveraged fund gets completely wiped out. Although such total goose eggs are rare, an inverse 3X fund that sought to triple the opposite of the daily return of Moderna stock went to zero last month on the London Stock Exchange. Total loss is less likely with lower leverage and broader underlying assets.

 

TQQQ launched Feb. 9, 2010, less than a year after stocks bottomed in the global financial crisis and a decade after the bubble in internet stocks burst.

 

That was a pretty good time to start counting! So was 2014, when my second reader bought in.

 

TQQQ isn’t old enough to have gone through two of the worst market bloodbaths in history. From the end of October 2007 to early March 2009, the Nasdaq-100 index lost 51.6%. From March 2000 to early October 2002, it sank a terrifying 82.4%.

 

How would a leveraged fund have performed if it had existed long enough to suffer multiples of those losses?

 

Many investors might not know that TQQQ has an older, slightly more conservative sibling: UltraNasdaq-100 ProFund. It’s a mutual fund, not an ETF, and it seeks to double rather than triple the Nasdaq-100 index’s daily returns.

 

Its track record just so happens to include both the global financial crisis and the bursting of the internet bubble.

 

The results (the fund is in blue, the index in green) are not pretty:

 
 
Performance of the UltraNasdaq-100 ProFund and the Nasdaq-100 index FACTSET
 

The leveraged fund earned an annualized average of 1.6 percentage points less than the underlying index over the long run—a cumulative gulf of more than 590 percentage points.

 

This period includes the full year of 1999, when the Nasdaq-100 doubled and the fund more than tripled.

 

To be fair, the mutual fund has much higher expenses than the TQQQ ETF, accounting for part of its underperformance—but not all.

 

So, if you bought TQQQ in 2010 or 2014 and have held it ever since, you are tough, and you’ve earned the right to crow about it. But you’re also lucky.

 

The past decade-and-a-half have been a Golden Age for leveraged funds: Interest rates were at rock-bottom until recently, and stocks boomed. But no Golden Age lasts forever, especially in markets. If rates keep going up and markets go down, the same leverage that magnified wealth on the way up will destroy it on the way down.
